question:
Patient note:
A 49-year-old man was driven to the emergency department at 01:20 after abruptly vomiting two cupfuls of bright red fluid mixed with partially digested dinner while brushing his teeth for the night; he described a metallic after-taste and mild burning in the retrosternal area that had bothered him intermittently for a week, especially on days when he delayed breakfast. The patient reports having passed an ordinary light-brown stool earlier that afternoon that flushed away without leaving a dark stain and has noticed no change in stool color, tarry texture, or foul asphaltic odor since the vomiting began. He feels slightly woozy when he stands quickly but has kept full awareness, has not toppled, and was able to walk unassisted from the parking lot into triage. Past medical record lists seasonal allergic rhinitis and chronic lumbar strain from warehouse work; he takes over-the-counter naproxen 440 mg twice daily for back discomfort, nightly famotidine 20 mg when heartburn flares, and no prescription anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, corticosteroids, or herbal supplements. He has never been told he has viral hepatitis, fatty liver, cirrhosis, jaundice, ascites, varices, alcohol--related injury, cardiomyopathy, reduced ejection fraction, or peripheral edema. Five months ago he completed a routine insurance physical with normal comprehensive metabolic profile, and his last exercise was a five-mile bike ride yesterday without chest pressure, shortness of breath, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or leg swelling afterwards. He drinks two bottles of beer on most weekends, has not smoked for twelve years after a 15-pack-year history, and denies recreational drug use. Family history reveals a mother with gastroesophageal reflux treated medically and a father who underwent coronary stenting at age 68; no relatives have bleeding disorders or chronic liver problems. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, weight loss, rash, easy bruising, flank pain, oliguria, or bowel habit change. Upon arrival—before any intravenous line, crystalloids, acid suppression, antiemetics, vasopressors, or blood products were started—he sat upright on the stretcher appearing anxious but talkative; breathing was unlabored. Triage vitals taken with the right arm at heart level showed a systolic blood pressure of 137 mm Hg, diastolic 84 mm Hg, pulse 77 beats per minute with a regular waveform on the monitor, respirations 16 per minute, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Skin was warm with brisk capillary refill; conjunctivae were pink, sclerae anicteric, and oral mucosa moist, bearing flecks of fresh red material along the uvula. Neck veins were flat at 45°, carotid upstrokes brisk, and peripheral pulses 2 + symmetric without pedal edema. Cardiac examination revealed a steady S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; point of maximal impulse was nondisplaced. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout with good aeration. Abdomen was flat, bowel sounds normoactive; gentle epigastric palpation elicited mild tenderness but no guarding, rebound, organomegaly, or pulsatile mass. There were no spider angiomas, palmar erythema, telangiectasias, or asterixis. A focused neurologic screen showed full orientation, equal and reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and steady gait observed as he transferred to the stretcher. Rectal examination was deferred until laboratory tubes were filled because the patient felt queasy, but there was no stool on the perianal skin. Two 18-gauge peripheral catheters were placed solely for phlebotomy; at this snapshot he had received no medications or fluids. Initial laboratory panel resulted twenty minutes later and, still prior to therapy, revealed hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, mean corpuscular volume 92 fL, platelet count 236 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 8.9 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 63 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (baseline unknown but presumed normal), sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, glucose 108 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 29 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, albumin 4.3 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.02. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 78 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography displayed clear lung fields and an unremarkable cardiac silhouette; a supine abdominal radiograph showed a nonspecific gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air. At this exact moment he remained nil per os, under continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring, and a type-and-screen had been sent to the blood bank while gastroenterology was paged for expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy to localize and control the suspected upper gastrointestinal source of his hematemesis.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses pretreatment laboratory values, vital signs, symptoms, and comorbidities:
- Urea: BUN 63 mg/dL corresponds to urea 63 ÷ 2.8 = 22.5 mmol/L. The 10 to <25 mmol/L tier scores 4 points.
- Hemoglobin: 14.5 g/dL, above the male scoring threshold of <13 g/dL → 0.
- Systolic blood pressure: 137 mmHg, above the scoring threshold of <110 mmHg → 0.
- Pulse ≥100/min (+1): pulse 77/min → 0.
- Melena (+1): brown stool without tarry discoloration → 0.
- Syncope (+2): lightheadedness without loss of consciousness → 0.
- Hepatic disease (+2): none reported → 0.
- Heart failure (+2): none reported → 0.
Sum: 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 4.
Final answer: 4
